syllabusRef: Investigative Study (AAC section of the specification, Descriptors of Quality)

notes.h: What the Investigative Study is and how it is weighted
notes.b: The Business Alive Investigative Study is a student-led research project that is assessed as part of the Leaving Certificate Business course. It rewards sustained independent work over the study period.
points: The study is assessed through the AAC section of the specification and is worth 40% of the overall marks, which is 200 marks.
The written examination is worth the remaining 60%, so the study carries a large share of the course's marks and must be planned from the start.
The study is marked against the Descriptors of Quality, which cover planning, investigating, applying and communicating.
The completed study is submitted to the teacher by 12 March 2027.
The study rewards the process of investigation as well as the final report, so the evidence of planning and monitoring matters.

notes.b: The SEC brief sets limits on length and images. Check the current brief for the exact counting rules before writing.
points: The report must be no more than 1,500 words, so each section should be planned to a word budget from the beginning.
No more than 10 images may be included, so each image must show evidence, such as a chart of primary data, rather than decorate the report.
Confirm in the SEC brief which elements, such as tables, captions or the reference list, count towards the word limit.
Use a consistent layout with clear headings for each report section, and a referenced list of sources at the end.

notes.b: The report is organised into five sections, each with a suggested word count. The content of each section follows from the study's stages.
points: Section one covers the research question, its SMART refinement and why it matters to the business or sector.
Section two covers the project plan and how the study was managed, including the risk assessment and monitoring.
Section three presents the findings from primary and secondary sources, with each source judged for credibility.
Section four analyses and evaluates the findings, states the limitations and identifies any gaps in the data.
Section five draws conclusions and recommendations for a named audience, and reflects on how the student's perspective changed.
Check the exact section headings, suggested word counts and mark allocation in the SEC brief, as these are set there and not in this summary.

notes.h: The six stages of the study
notes.b: The stages form a learning sequence. Each stage produces the evidence that the next stage uses.
points: Getting started: choose a business topic linked to the 2027 digital work practice theme and note initial ideas.
Developing a question: refine the ideas into one SMART research question with a clear business focus.
Project plan: set the purpose, goals, criteria for success, roles, resources, objectives, time schedule, risk assessment and monitoring arrangements.
Sources and data: gather primary and secondary data, judge each source, and record and acknowledge everything as the work proceeds.
Analysis and evaluation: interpret the data, evaluate the findings and perspectives, and identify gaps and limitations.
Applying learning and conclusions: state conclusions and recommendations for a named audience, and reflect on the change in perspective.

notes.b: The planning descriptor rewards a focused question and a plan that is followed and adjusted when needed.
points: High achievement shows a research question that passes the SMART tests, rather than a broad topic label.
The plan has every required element with realistic timings, rather than a list of vague intentions.
Monitoring evidence shows the plan was checked and changed where needed, with dated entries in the investigative folder.

notes.b: The investigating descriptor rewards the range of sources and the judgement applied to them.
points: High achievement draws on several primary and secondary sources from differing perspectives, and explains why each was chosen.
Each source is judged for credibility, context, accuracy, bias, reliability and value, and that judgement is visible in the report.
Data is recorded and referenced, checked for representativeness, and any gaps are identified with their likely effect on the conclusions.

notes.b: The applying descriptor rewards the use of business concepts and evidence to reach supported decisions.
points: High achievement applies business concepts to the specific business and question, rather than describing the concepts in general terms.
Analysis explains causes and effects, and evaluation weighs the findings against stated criteria to reach a judgement.
Conclusions and recommendations follow directly from the evidence and name a specific audience and a specific action.

notes.b: The communicating descriptor rewards a clear, well-structured report suited to its audience.
points: High achievement uses headings that follow the research question, so the reader can follow the argument from question to conclusion.
Charts and graphs are labelled, suited to the data, and referred to in the text.
Writing is precise, uses correct business terms, and stays within the word and image limits.
References are consistent and complete, and every in-text citation matches an entry in the reference list.

notes.h: The 2027 topic: a digital work practice
notes.b: The 2027 topic asks students to investigate a digital work practice and its impact on employers or employees. Examples include remote working, cloud collaboration and automation.
points: A digital work practice is a way of working that relies on digital tools, such as video calls for meetings or cloud platforms for shared files.
The impact can fall on employers, such as costs, productivity or recruitment, or on employees, such as flexibility, workload or skills needs.
A strong study narrows to one practice, one business or sector, and one affected group, so that the research question remains testable.
The later chapters on digital transformation, and on how technology affects employees, provide the background theory for this topic.

notes.b: Good work is shown by the student's own process, sources and judgement. Quality guidance describes what to aim for, and is not a template for a report.
points: Good work has a research question the student can answer, evidence the student collected or found, and a conclusion the evidence supports.
Strong studies show visible decisions, such as dropping a source after judging it unreliable and explaining why.
Weak work typically describes a topic in general terms, copies published content without acknowledgement, or reaches conclusions the data cannot support.
Work written by another person, or generated by a tool and presented as the student's own, is not acceptable and breaches the rules on authentication.

keyTerms.definition: A student-led research project in which the student plans, investigates, analyses and reports on a business question, assessed as part of the Leaving Certificate.
The criteria the SEC uses to judge the Investigative Study, covering planning, investigating, applying and communicating.
The focused question the study sets out to answer, tested against SMART criteria before data collection begins.
The process by which a teacher confirms that the submitted work is the student's own.
A way of doing work that depends on digital tools, such as remote working, cloud collaboration or automation.
Recording and crediting every source used, including any artificial intelligence tools, within the report.
Using business concepts and evidence to reach supported conclusions and recommendations for a specific audience.
A specific proposed action for a named audience that follows from the conclusions reached.
The upper limit on the number of words in the report, set in the SEC brief for the 2027 study.

questions.prompt: Explain what the investigating descriptor rewards, and describe what high achievement looks like for a study of a digital work practice.
questions.model: The investigating descriptor rewards the range of sources used and the judgement applied to them. High achievement draws on several primary and secondary sources from different perspectives, such as employees, managers and independent reports on the practice, and explains why each source was chosen. Each source is judged for credibility, context, accuracy, bias, reliability and value, and this judgement is visible in the report rather than assumed. Data is recorded and referenced at the time it is gathered, checked for whether it represents the group studied, and any gaps are identified with a note of how they affect the conclusions.

questions.prompt: Explain why a project plan with a risk assessment and a monitoring record strengthens an Investigative Study.
questions.model: A project plan with a risk assessment shows that the student considered what could disrupt the study and prepared responses in advance, which is the basis of the planning descriptor. A monitoring record shows the plan was checked against progress, with dated entries recording problems and the changes made, so the student can show the study was managed rather than improvised. Together these give evidence of the process, which the marks for the study reward alongside the final report.

questions.prompt: State two rules on formatting that a student must follow in the report, and explain why each matters.
questions.model: The report must be no more than 1,500 words, which requires a word budget for each section so that the report stays focused and the marking is fair to every student. No more than 10 images may be included, so each image must justify its place by showing evidence rather than decoration, which keeps the report concise and clearly based on the student's own findings.
